explanation:
The 'override' identifier is a feature introduced in Modern C++ to explicitly state a developer's intent that a member function in a derived class is meant to override a virtual function from a base class. By adding this specifier, you enlist the compiler to verify this relationship, turning potential runtime logic errors into clear, actionable compile-time errors.

Scott Meyers emphasizes that using 'override' is a critical practice for robust object-oriented design. Its primary purpose is to prevent a common and difficult-to-diagnose category of bugs where a derived class function *appears* to override a base class virtual function but fails to do so due to a subtle signature mismatch—such as a typo in the name, a difference in const-qualification, or incorrect parameter types. Without 'override', this mistake results in the base class function being called when the derived one was expected, a silent failure that can be very hard to debug.

The mechanics are straightforward: when the compiler encounters 'override' at the end of a member function declaration, it checks the inheritance hierarchy for a base class containing a virtual function with the exact same signature. If no such function exists, the compilation fails. This transforms a developer's intention into a verifiable contract. A key aspect of 'override' is that it is a *contextual keyword*, not a reserved one. This means it only has special meaning in this specific grammatical context, ensuring that it doesn't break legacy code that might use the word 'override' as a variable or non-virtual function name.

In practice, consistently using 'override' for all overriding functions makes class hierarchies significantly more maintainable and self-documenting. It provides an explicit declaration of intent, which is invaluable during code reviews and refactoring. If a base class virtual function's signature is ever changed, the compiler will immediately flag all derived classes that attempt to override the old signature, guiding the developer to make the necessary updates.

A common pitfall is simply neglecting to use it out of old habit, thereby forgoing the compiler's protection. It's also important to remember that 'override' is only applicable to virtual functions; it cannot be used to detect the accidental hiding of non-virtual base class functions, which is a separate issue.
practical_example: During a large-scale refactoring, a virtual method in a base class is changed from taking an integer to a long. Without 'override', all derived classes would silently fail to override the new method, creating subtle bugs. With 'override', the compiler generates an error for every derived class, creating a clear to-do list for the developer to update the system correctly.
keywords: C++ override keyword, override specifier, explicit virtual function, virtual function checking
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
